A medal race across eight editions
Each line tracks a country’s cumulative team medals from Atlanta to Paris. Use the filters to focus on a country or event; hover over a point for the edition-by-edition total. Every podium finish counts once for its pair and event.






Country

Cumulative beach volleyball team medals by country and event, 1996–2024. Source: olympicAthletes through 2016 and official Olympic results for 2020 and 2024.



Sources: olympicAthletes through 2016 and official Olympic results for Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. The 48 medal-team results are converted to 240 cumulative country/event/year values; zero-medal years are shown as zero, not as extra medal results.

title: About
text:
Kaitlin Powell is a collegiate beach volleyball athlete at New College of Florida who wanted to combine her passion for the sport with data analysis. This website grew from that interest, bringing together the sport and an examination of its Olympic history.



This project explores Olympic beach volleyball participation, international success, athlete characteristics, and historical trends. It follows the sport across the eight Olympic editions represented in the analysis, from Atlanta 1996 through Paris 2024, and presents patterns in participation, age, country performance, and medals.



The original dataset is olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes, a package dataset containing 315,094 Olympic athlete-event observations. After filtering for Summer Games beach-volleyball events, the project uses 756 athlete-event records.
The filtered observations cover 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020, and 2024. Relevant variables include athlete ID, name, sex, age, height, weight, team, NOC, Games, year, season, city, sport, event, and medal status.
For 1996–2016, medals come from the athlete dataset. The project also uses official Tokyo 2020 beach volleyball results and official Paris 2024 beach volleyball results to add team-medal results for those editions.



The data was cleaned and filtered in R by retaining Summer Games records for the Volleyball sport and matching beach-volleyball event names. Where useful, team identifiers were standardized to country labels, missing or unavailable values were left unassigned, and selected visualizations were summarized by year, country, sex, or athlete characteristics.
The project distinguishes three units of analysis:



Each row represents an athlete in a particular Games and event. An athlete who competed at more than one Olympics appears in more than one row.



Unique-athlete counts use source athlete IDs. This number does not equal participation totals because one athlete may have records from multiple Olympic editions.



Medal totals count one medal-winning team per Games, event, and medal. The two athletes on a pair are not counted as two separate medals.


Indoor volleyball is included in the homepage comparison because it provides historical context for age patterns across both volleyball disciplines. The comparison is based on Summer Olympic Volleyball records rather than on beach volleyball alone.



Some records have missing data, including athlete characteristics such as height. In addition, 171 of the 192 source beach-volleyball records from 2020 and 2024 lack a country that can be derived from the team field, so the country participation map is limited to 1996–2016. Missing identifiers are not replaced through inference.
Historical patterns show associations and changes over time, but they do not establish causation. Differences among Games, athletes, countries, data coverage, and Olympic rules should be considered when interpreting trends.



The website is built with R, the tidyverse and ggplot2, plotly, crosstalk, and leaflet. Quarto renders the pages and their analyses, and GitHub hosts the source project.


View the project repository on GitHub

text:
Atlanta 1996 — Paris 2024



From Atlanta to Paris, discover the athletes, nations, and podium moments that shaped Olympic beach volleyball.

Explore the data →

title: Olympic Beach Volleyball: Road to Gold
section: Olympic volleyball ages, at a glance
text:
Olympic volleyball ages, at a glance
Each point is one age-reported person-event record. Beach volleyball is highlighted; indoor Volleyball provides historical context. Small, seeded jitter separates overlapping points without adding or removing records.




Source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes. Each point is one age-reported Summer Olympic Volleyball athlete-event record (4,783 of 4,792); gold highlights all 756 beach volleyball records from 1996–2024.



Key takeaway: The median recorded age is 29 for beach volleyball and 25 for indoor Volleyball. The oldest source record is age 73—the axis previously rounded up to 75 for its five-year tick marks.

One point represents a person listed for one Games and event—not a unique athlete across their career. The chart contains 4,783 records from 3,448 distinct source IDs; repeat Olympians therefore appear more than once. The source’s oldest indoor Volleyball entries include coaching staff (for example, Antonio Giacobbe at age 73), so these genuine records are retained but should not be read as player ages. The source does not identify participant roles.


New to beach volleyball?


The game in a few serves


Two players, one team
Each side fields a pair on a sand court. Teammates work together to keep the ball in play and send it over the net.


Rally scoring
A point is awarded after every rally. Matches are best of three sets: the first two go to 21 points, and a deciding set, if needed, goes to 15. A team must win a set by two points.


From pools to podium
In recent Olympic editions, teams begin in pool play before the knockout rounds. Qualification details vary by Games; every edition ends with one medal-winning team in each event for gold, silver, and bronze.




Continue to Olympic Trends to compare participation across Summer Games.
Sources: olympicAthletes package and data documentation. See methodology and results sources for team-medal counting and the recent podium supplement.

text:
One Olympic timeline, three lenses
The broadest view follows every Summer Olympic athlete-event entry. The gold trace then zooms in: first on all indoor and beach Volleyball entries, then on beach volleyball alone, identified from the event field. Each panel has its own vertical scale so the specialist event remains visible.

Athlete ages across the Games
These points show individual beach-volleyball athlete-event records, not yearly averages. The spread reveals the age range within each event and how it changes across editions.




Each point is one of 756 beach-volleyball athlete-event records from 1996–2024. Source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes.



Source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes; 756 athlete-event rows from 1996–2024. Age is present for every beach-volleyball record in this source.

Because each marker is a real athlete-event record, repeated appearances by the same athlete in different editions remain separate rows and are not synthetic extra observations.






NoteWhat counts as a record?



One row represents one athlete at one Games edition in one event—not one unique person or one team. Beach volleyball is filtered from event within the Volleyball sport, rather than treating all Volleyball entries as beach volleyball.


The Men vs. Women page focuses on beach volleyball participation and podiums by event.

title: Road to Gold
text:
Brazil has earned 14 team medals, three more than the United States with 11. That is the most sustained success in the Olympic beach volleyball medal table, but the podium is not limited to two countries: 15 countries have won a medal.
Brazil reached the podium at every Games from 1996 through 2016, then returned to the top of the women’s podium in Paris. The United States has more golds, while Brazil’s seven silvers match the U.S. total of seven golds. More recent editions brought men’s golds for Norway in Tokyo and Sweden in Paris.

How countries’ medal totals changed across editions
This interactive timeline follows each country’s cumulative team medals from Atlanta to Paris. Hover for the medals earned in an edition and the running total; click countries in the legend to focus the comparison.




Cumulative beach-volleyball team medals by country across eight Olympic editions. Each line is a country; zero-medal editions remain at the previous cumulative total.

title: Road to Gold
text:
The athletes behind the podium
This athlete-level view shows age by Olympic edition for beach volleyball competitors. Every age-reported beach-volleyball record is included; color distinguishes the men’s and women’s events.




Beach volleyball athlete-event records by age, event, and Olympic year. Source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes.



Observation count: 756 athlete-event records produce 756 points, representing 520 distinct source IDs. All 756 beach-volleyball records in the source have reported ages.

The median age is 29. A point is one person’s participation in one Games and event; an athlete who returns in later editions appears again, so the points are records, not unique people.

title: Road to Gold
text:
Methodology

The source is olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes, a 315,094-row, 16-column athlete-event dataset. The package describes 1896–2016 records as extending the Olympic history dataset, with later records sourced from Olympedia.
Beach volleyball is selected by requiring sport == "Volleyball" and a beach-volleyball match in event. The package’s 4,792-row volleyball_athletes subset contains indoor and beach volleyball; it is not used as a beach-volleyball count.
For 1996–2016, the source repeats the medal on both athletes’ rows. We retain one row for each Games year, event, team identifier, and medal, then normalize team suffixes (such as -1) only when aggregating results by country.
The package data used here has no beach-volleyball medal labels for 2020 or 2024. We add the six podium teams for each of those editions from the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 official results pages. These are team-level rows, so no athlete-level medal duplication is introduced.
Participation charts count athlete-event rows; medal charts count medal-winning teams. A pair therefore contributes two participation records but only one medal.
To render the site, install R packages olympicAthletes, tidyverse, ggplot2, plotly, crosstalk, leaflet, rnaturalearth, and geojsonsf, then run quarto render.

For other country results, edition details, and filters, head to Country Explorer.

title: Men vs Women
text:
Since 2000, the men’s and women’s events each have 48 athlete-event records at every Games; in 1996, the women’s event had 36 compared with 48 for men. Across all editions, the median recorded age is 30 for men and 28 for women. Each event has earned 24 team medals.
An athlete-event record is one person’s participation in one Games and event, not a unique athlete. The 756 age records represent 520 distinct source IDs; returning athletes appear in more than one record.


The distributions overlap substantially. The median age is 30 in the men’s event and 28 in the women’s event; each dot is one real source record.




One point per beach-volleyball athlete-event record with reported age. Source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes.



Observation count: 756 age-reported athlete-event records and the same number of plotted points; 520 distinct source IDs. All beach-volleyball records in this source have an age.




This height-versus-age view retains the existing individual profiles. Points are colored by event and shaped by medal status where the source reports it.




Source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes. Shows 668 of 756 athlete-event records with reported height; medal status is unavailable in the source for 2020 and 2024.



Observation count: 668 of 756 athlete-event records have reported age and height and are plotted; 88 lack height. Medal status is not reported by this source for 2020 or 2024.




Height is reported for 668 of 756 athlete-event records. That is enough for a descriptive comparison, but missing heights are noted rather than assumed to match the observed records.




One point per beach-volleyball athlete-event record with reported height. Heights are in centimeters; source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes.



Observation count: 668 reported heights are plotted: 343 men’s and 325 women’s records. Height is missing for 88 records (41 men and 47 women). Median recorded height is 193 cm for men and 180 cm for women.








Athlete-event participation by event and Olympic year. Source: olympicAthletes::olympic_athletes.



Observation count: 756 athlete-event records are aggregated to 16 year-by-event points (eight editions and two events). These counts measure listed participation, not audience or popularity.








Each point is one of 48 medal-winning country-teams. Panels compare men’s and women’s results by Olympic year; 2020 and 2024 podiums use official Olympic results.



Sources: olympicAthletes for 1996–2016; official Olympic results for Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. The plot shows all 48 country-team medal results once each, not once per athlete.

Observation count: 48 medal-winning country-teams produce 48 points, 24 per event. Brazil leads both tallies (8 women’s and 6 men’s medals), while the United States has 7 women’s and 4 men’s; Australia’s three medals are all in the women’s event. These are team results, not individual athlete medals.
